title: Tuning and evaluating a random forest regressor

items.stem: A random forest regressor with 100 trees is retrained with 1,000 trees, and nothing else changes. What usually happens to its error on held-out data?

options.text: It rises, because the forest now overfits the training data
It falls a little, then levels off with no overfitting penalty
It keeps falling by a similar amount for every tree added
It stays exactly the same, because trees never affect error

items.stem: Each tree in a forest is trained on a bootstrap sample: n rows drawn with replacement from n training rows. For a large n, about what percentage of the training rows is left out of any one tree's sample (the rows used for out-of-bag evaluation)? Give a percentage to one decimal place.
A random forest has a training R² of 0.98 but an out-of-bag R² of 0.62, with min_samples_leaf=1 and 200 trees. Which single change is most likely to narrow this gap?

options.text: Lower min_samples_leaf so each tree fits the data more closely
Raise n_estimators from 200 to 20,000 to average more trees
Raise min_samples_leaf so each leaf averages more training rows
Raise max_features so every split can consider every feature

items.stem: In one or two sentences, explain why setting max_features to a fraction of the features (rather than all of them) can lower a random forest's error, even though each individual tree gets weaker.
You run a cross-validated grid search over several hyperparameters and pick the best setting. You want an honest estimate of how this model will perform on new data. Which number should you report?

options.text: The best cross-validation score found during the grid search
The R² of the refit best model on its own training data
The average cross-validation score over all the settings tried
The score of the best model on a test set never used in tuning

items.stem: On a held-out test set, a forest's squared prediction errors sum to 20 (SSE). The squared differences between the test targets and their mean sum to 80 (SST). What is the forest's test R², computed as 1 - SSE/SST? Give a number, not a percentage.
